en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses
9. The Second Training Rule on Maliciousness At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, while the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka were descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, they saw a he-goat misbehaving with a she-goat.
Having seen this, they said:
"Come, friends, let us make this goat Dabba Mallaputta by name,
and let us make this she-goat Mettiyā a bhikkhunī."
"In this way we shall speak:
'Friends, previously we spoke of Dabba Mallaputta on the basis of what we had heard;
but now we have seen him with our own eyes acting improperly toward the bhikkhunī Mettiyā.'"
They made that goat named Dabba Mallaputta;
they made that she-goat the nun named Mettiyā.
They informed the monks.
“Friends, previously we spoke of Dabba Mallaputta based on what we had heard.
But now we have seen with our own eyes how he behaved improperly toward the bhikkhunī Mettiyā.
Thus the bhikkhus said.
“Friends, do not speak thus.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta will not do such a thing.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and for this reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Do you remember, Dabba, doing such a thing as these monks have said?
“I do not remember, Bhante, doing anything of the sort, as the Blessed One knows me.”
A second time, and a third time, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Dabba, do you remember doing such a thing as these bhikkhus have said?”
“As the Blessed One knows me, venerable sir.
“Dabba, those who are truly worthy do not evade in this way.
If it was done by you, say, ‘It was done by me.’”
“If you have not done it, say that you have not done it.
“Venerable sir, since I was born, I do not recall ever having engaged in sexual intercourse even in a dream, let alone while awake.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “In that case, bhikkhus, investigate these bhikkhus.”
Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then those monks questioned the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks.
While being questioned by the monks, they reported this matter to the monks:

“But, friends, did you accuse the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) on account of some minor point or mere pretext taken from a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belonging to a different category?
“It is so, friend.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ... complained, grumbled, and became indignant:

“How indeed can the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, on account of some minor point or mere pretext from a legal issue belonging to one category, accuse the venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense involving defeat?
Then those monks, having rebuked the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...

“Is it true, monks, that you have charged Dabba Mallaputta with an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), on the basis of some minor point or mere pretext from a legal issue belonging to a different category?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
“How indeed, you foolish men, could you, on account of some minor point or mere pretext from a legal issue belonging to one category, accuse Dabba Mallaputta of an offense entailing expulsion?
This, foolish men, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence… And furthermore,
monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:”
“Whatever monk, being angry, resentful, and displeased with another monk, should, on account of some minor point or pretext related to a legal issue concerning something else,
accuse him of an offense entailing expulsion, thinking, ‘Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life.’”

Then, at a later time, whether being pressed for an explanation or not being pressed for an explanation, that legal issue turns out to be one belonging to a different category, such that only a slight portion was taken up as a pretext, yet the monk maintains his position of fault; this is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
"Whoever" means whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context. "Bhikkhunī" [is explained in the same manner].
Another monk.
"Hating" means being angry,
displeased, dissatisfied, with a mind struck down and harboring resentment.
“Displeased” means that because of that anger, that hatred, that dissatisfaction, and that lack of contentment, he is displeased.
“Of a legal issue pertaining to something else” means:
It is either "belonging to a different category from an offense" or "belonging to a different category from a legal issue.
How is a legal issue belonging to a different category from another legal issue?
A legal issue arising from a dispute is of a different category from a legal issue arising from an accusation, a legal issue arising from an offense, and a legal issue arising from business.
A legal issue concerning an accusation is distinct from a legal issue concerning an offense, a legal issue concerning business, and a legal issue concerning a dispute.
A legal issue concerning an offense is distinct from a legal issue concerning business, a legal issue concerning a dispute, and a legal issue concerning an accusation.
A legal issue concerning business is distinct from a legal issue concerning a dispute, a legal issue concerning an accusation, and a legal issue concerning an offense.
Thus, one legal issue is extraneous to another legal issue.
How is a legal issue related to another legal issue?
A legal issue arising from a dispute is related to a legal issue arising from a dispute.
A legal issue arising from censure is of the same category as a legal issue arising from censure.
A legal issue arising from an offense may be of the same category as a legal issue arising from an offense, or it may be of a different category.
How is a legal issue arising from an offense of a different category from a legal issue arising from an offense?

An offense involving unchastity (methunadhamma-pārājika) is distinct from an offense involving taking what is not given (adinnādāna-pārājika), an offense involving a human being (manussaviggaha-pārājika), and an offense involving a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma-pārājika).
An offense involving taking what is not given is distinct from an offense involving a human being, an offense involving a superhuman state, and an offense involving unchastity.
An offense involving a human being is distinct from an offense involving a superhuman state, an offense involving unchastity, and an offense involving taking what is not given.

An offense involving a defeat concerning superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma-pārājika-āpatti*) is distinct from an offense involving a defeat concerning sexual intercourse (*methuna-dhamma-pārājika-āpatti*), an offense involving a defeat concerning theft (*adinnādāna-pārājika-āpatti*), and an offense involving a defeat concerning one who resembles a human (*manussaviggaha-pārājika-āpatti*).
Thus, a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is distinct from another legal issue arising from an offense.
How is a legal issue arising from an offense related to another legal issue arising from an offense? It is as follows: [the following offenses are related].
An offense of defeat involving sexual intercourse is similar to an offense of defeat involving sexual intercourse.
An offense of defeat involving taking what is not given is similar to an offense of defeat involving taking what is not given.
An offense of defeat involving a human being is similar to an offense of defeat involving a human being.
An offense of defeat involving a superhuman state is similar to an offense of defeat involving a superhuman state.
Thus, a legal issue arising from an offense is similar to a legal issue arising from an offense.
A legal issue concerning business is similar to a legal issue concerning business.
In this way, one legal issue is related to another legal issue.
"Taking some part, even a mere fraction" refers to the ten fractions:

the fraction of birth, the fraction of name, the fraction of clan, the fraction of gender, the fraction of offense, the fraction of bowl, the fraction of robe, the fraction of preceptor, the fraction of teacher, and the fraction of lodging.
A "caste-remnant" (jātileso) is a khattiya seen committing an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Having seen another khattiya, he accuses him:
“I have seen a khattiya.
You have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan.”
“There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you,” if he says this,
there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa for every statement.
It is the same if a brahmin has been seen … [and so forth].
A vaiśya is seen ... [and so on] ...
a śūdra is seen committing an offense entailing defeat.
Seeing another person who is a *sudda*, he accuses him:
"I have seen a *sudda*.
You have committed an offense entailing defeat; you are no longer an ascetic, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son... [and so forth].
There is an offense of Saṅghādisesa through speech, by means of speech.
A mere trace of a name, such as "Buddharakkhita," is seen... [and so forth].
Dhammarakkhita was seen... [and so on] ...
Saṅgharakkhita was seen committing an offense entailing expulsion.
Having seen another Saṅgharakkhita, he accused him:
“I have seen Saṅgharakkhita.
You have committed an offense entailing expulsion; you are no longer a monastic, you are no longer a son of the Sakyan. … [as above] … There is an offense for each statement;
for each statement, there is an offense entailing suspension.”
Gotama named Godhāya was seen...
Moggallāna was seen... [and so on].
Kaccāyana was seen...
[and so on] ...Vāsiṭṭha was seen committing an offense entailing expulsion.
Having seen another Vāsiṭṭha, he accuses him:
“I have seen you, Vāsiṭṭha.
You have committed an offense entailing defeat; you are no longer an ascetic, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son...
[as before] ...there is an offense for every utterance, a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) for every utterance.”
The characteristic mark is seen as long …pe… it is seen as short …pe…
He is seen as black...
[and so on] ...he is seen as white while committing an offense entailing defeat.
Having seen someone else who is white, he accuses him—
“I have seen you clearly.
You have committed an offense entailing defeat; you are no longer a recluse, nor a follower of the Sakyan son...
There is an offense on each word; for every word, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.”
"A trace of an offense" means that one is seen committing a light offense;
if he then accuses him of a *pārājika* offense—
“You are not an ascetic; you are not a follower of the Sakyan son.
… [as before] … There is an offense by speech: an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) by speech.
What is called “a smear on the bowl”?
He is seen wearing an iron bowl …pe… he is seen wearing a cloth bowl …pe… he is seen wearing a *sumbhaka* bowl while committing an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
Seeing another wearing a *sumbhaka* bowl, he accuses him:
“I have seen you wearing a *sumbhaka* bowl.
You have committed an offense entailing defeat; you are no longer a recluse, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son…” [and so on].
There is an offense of Saṅghādisesa by means of speech, through speech.
"A trace of robe-cloth" means that a wearer of rag-robes has been seen... [and so on].
He was seen wearing a householder’s robe while committing an offense entailing expulsion.
Upon seeing another person wearing a householder’s robe, he accuses him, saying:
"I saw one wearing a householder’s robe."
"You have committed an offense entailing expulsion; you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son...
[as above] ...there is an offense for every word, for every word there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
This is called 'having the semblance of a preceptor.'"
The co-resident of such-and-such a person was seen committing an offense entailing expulsion.
Having seen another co-resident of such-and-such a person, he accuses him, saying:
"I saw the co-resident of such-and-such a person."
"You have committed an offense entailing expulsion; you are no longer an ascetic, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son...
[as above] ...there is an offense for every word; for every word there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
This is called a 'trace of the teacher'."
"I saw the pupil of such-and-such a person committing an offense entailing expulsion.
Having seen another pupil of such-and-such a person, I accuse him:
'I saw the pupil of such-and-such a person.'"
"You have committed an offense entailing expulsion; you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son...
...an offense is incurred for every utterance, [namely] a saṅghādisesa for each utterance.
"A mere trace of a lodging" means:
A certain person staying at a particular residence was seen committing an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
Having seen another person staying at that same residence, he accuses him, saying:
"I saw a certain person staying at this residence."
“You have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan son;
there is no Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremony, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha, together with you.”
The offense is by speech; it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.
"By a *pārājika* offense" means by one of the four [pārājikas].
"Anuddhaṁseyya" means:
he either accuses him or causes him to be accused,
thinking, "Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life."
I would fall away from the state of a bhikkhu, I would fall away from the duty of a recluse, I would fall away from the aggregate of virtue, and I would fall away from the qualities of asceticism.
"At a later time" means:
when that moment, that instant, that brief duration during which one has been accused has passed.
"Being interrogated" means being interrogated regarding that very matter on account of which he has been accused.
"Not being interrogated" means [the opposite].
Not being spoken to by anyone.
"Legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to four legal issues:
the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"A certain region is slightly affected by a stain" means that one of those stains has been taken up.
And the bhikkhu stands upon hatred.
"Something empty was spoken by me; something false was spoken by me; something unreal was spoken by me; it was spoken by me without knowing.
It is a *saṅghādisesa*...
...therefore it is called "a *saṅghādisesa*."
A bhikkhu is seen committing an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa); he perceives that offense as one entailing suspension.
If someone then accuses him of a defeat (pārājika), saying:
"You are no longer an ascetic; you are no longer a son of the Sakyan," [he is not guilty of a formal act of accusation].

“There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you,” even so it is an offense belonging to another category, a slight transgression is committed, and there is an offense by speech: a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.
A bhikkhu is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense, yet he holds the view that it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) within the context of a *saṅghādisesa*... [and so forth].

there is a view that it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) … there is a view that it is an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) … there is a view that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) …
There is the view that it is a minor offense of wrong speech.
If one then accuses him of an offense entailing defeat:
"You are no longer a monastic... [and so on].
In this way, it is an offense belonging to another category, and a trace has been taken up: there is an offense by speech, namely a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.

A bhikkhu is seen committing a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), and he holds the view that it is a grave offense … [and so on] … he holds the view that it is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) regarding a grave offense.
There is the view that it is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya);
there is the view that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
there is the view that it is an offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita).
He holds the view that it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
If one then accuses him of a *pārājika* offense, saying: "You are not a recluse... [and so forth].
In this way too, it is an offense belonging to a different category, and a trace has been taken up: there is an offense by speech, namely a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.
For a monk, it is a *pācittiya*...
[and so on] ...a *pāṭidesanīya*.

He is seen committing an offense of wrong-doing; he holds the view that what is ill-spoken is ill-spoken … [and so on] … he holds the view that what is ill-spoken is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

there is a view that it is a grave offense (thullaccaya) … there is a view that it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) … there is a view that it is an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) …
There is the view that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one then accuses him of a defeat (pārājika), saying:
"You are not a recluse; you are not a son of the Sakyan," [he is guilty of a dukkaṭa].
‘There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you,’ even this is an offense of a different category;
a slight fault has been committed, and there is an offense by speech: a Saṅghādisesa by speech.
Having made each [phrase] a root, the wheel should be bound.
A bhikkhu is seen committing an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), and he perceives that offense as one involving suspension.
If someone then accuses him of a defeat (pārājika), saying:
"You are no longer an ascetic... [and so forth].
In this way too, it is an offense belonging to another category, and a trace has been taken up; there is an offense by speech, a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.
A bhikkhu is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense, yet he holds the view that it is a *thullaccaya* ...
[or] he holds the view that it is a *pācittiya*.
There is the view that it is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya);
there is the view that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
there is the view that it is an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita).
If he accuses him of an offense entailing expulsion,

saying, “You are no longer a monastic… [as before]… in this way it is an offense of a different category and a stain has been taken up; there is an offense for every word, a *saṅghādisesa* for every word.”

A bhikkhu is seen committing a *thullaccaya* offense; he regards the *thullaccaya* as a *thullaccaya* offense … [and so on] … he regards the *thullaccaya* as a *pācittiya* offense … he regards it as a *pāṭidesanīya* offense …
There is the view that it is an offense of wrong-doing;
there is the view that it is an offense of improper speech;
there is the view that it is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
If he accuses him of an offense entailing expulsion, saying, "You are no longer a monastic...
[and so forth], even though this is an offense of a different category and only a slight charge has been taken up, there is an offense for every word; for every word, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
For a bhikkhu, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) … [and so on] … an offense of acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) … an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) …

One who has committed an offense of wrong speech is seen [committing it]; one has the view that what is wrong speech is wrong speech … [and so on] … one has the view that what is wrong speech is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
one has the view that it is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
There is a view that it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya);
there is a view that it is an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya);
there is a view that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he accuses him of an offense entailing defeat, saying:
"You are no longer a recluse, you are no longer a son of the Sakyan;
for you there is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha together with you."
In this way, it is an offense belonging to another category, and a trace has been taken up; there is an offense by speech, a *saṅghādisesa* offense by speech.
There is no offense if, perceiving it as such, one reproaches or causes another to reproach [the person].
"In the case of one who is insane, and in the case of the first offender.
(The Section on Different Categories. The ninth training rule concerning minor faults is concluded.
